title: Another Weapon in the Nutrient Arms Race in Cells
content: Anyone who grew up in a large family can attest that at the dinner table competition for food can be fierce. In biological systems, competition for nutrients can be equally as fierce, and living cells have developed means of regulating which organelles get which nutrients. When cells are invaded by outside organisms, like microbes and parasites, the invaders need to utilize the cells’ nutrient stores for energy to survive and reproduce. Meanwhile, cells have developed mechanisms to limit invaders from accessing the needed nutrients. A classic example of this is the sequestration by immune cells of metal ions, such as iron, needed by bacteria to grow and thrive. By limiting access to these nutrients, the cell can reduce or eliminate the infectious potential of the invader [1]. This process is called nutritional immunity.
